title: Signature Big-Type Weaver
body:
The Signature Big-Type Weaver is an original Signature design that treats text size as a living setting, not a one-time switch. It watches which screens the user enlarges by hand, learns the comfortable size per app, and gently offers that size the next time the app opens, always with one tap to accept or decline. It never shrinks text on its own, never hides a control to make room, and keeps a large-print summary of what it changed, so the user stays in charge of their own screen. The design is labeled Signature throughout, and it is a design, not a shipped product claim.

How to do it: Offer the learned size per app with one-tap accept or decline; Never shrink text automatically; Never hide a control to make room; Keep a large-print change summary; Let any offer be dismissed permanently for that app.

What to check: Test the Weaver with a user who enlarges text by hand in three apps, and confirm it offers each learned size exactly once and accepts a decline without asking again.

When to stop or get help: Do not ship the Weaver if it ever shrinks text, hides a control, or nags after a decline. A helper that overrides its user is a hindrance, however clever its learning.

Put it into practice on a small, low-stakes example first, so the routine is familiar before you need it under pressure. For this record, that means trying the steps once in a calm moment, with no deadline and no audience, and noticing which step feels hardest. The hardest step is usually the one worth practising twice, because pressure does not create new skills, it reveals the ones you have already rehearsed. Write down what you checked and what you found, because a check that leaves no note is hard to repeat and harder to trust later, and because a short note lets someone else pick up where you left off.

Share the routine with the people who will use it with you, so that stopping, checking, and asking for help are normal steps, not signs of failure. Agree in advance what you will do when a check fails, so that a failed check leads to a pause and a fix rather than an argument or a quiet decision to carry on anyway. Review the routine after a month of use and change the parts that did not work in practice, keeping the parts that did. A routine that is reviewed stays alive; a routine that is never reviewed slowly becomes a poster on a wall.

title: Signature Clear-Voice Speaker
body:
The Signature Clear-Voice Speaker is an original Signature design for making spoken output easier to follow: it slows speech slightly, separates words more clearly, and repeats the important noun in a sentence, such as a name or a time, without being asked. It is designed for announcements, reminders, and read-aloud messages, where understanding the first time matters more than sounding natural. It keeps a plain on-off switch and a speed control with large labels, and it never raises volume as a substitute for clarity. The design is labeled Signature throughout.

What to check: Test the Speaker by reading a reminder with a name and a time, and confirm a listener repeats both back correctly on the first hearing.

When to stop or get help: Do not use the Speaker for urgent alerts that need a human voice or a siren. Slowed speech is for understanding, not for emergencies.

title: Signature Speak-to-Do Helper
body:
The Signature Speak-to-Do Helper is an original Signature design for voice commands that always show their work: every spoken command appears as large text on screen, waits for a nod or a tap, and only then acts, with an easy undo for the next minute. title: Signature Gentle-Colours Mode
body:

title: Signature Magnifier Companion

title: Signature Steady-Tap Aid
body:
The Signature Steady-Tap Aid is an original Signature design that forgives unsteady hands: it waits a beat longer for a tap to settle, treats a trembling double tap as one tap, and enlarges the nearest target when a tap lands between two buttons, asking which was meant instead of guessing. It learns the user's rhythm over days and adjusts its patience gradually, always showing what it changed in plain words. The design is labeled Signature throughout.

What to check: Test the Aid with a user whose taps often double, and confirm accidental double taps fall to near zero while intended double taps still work.

When to stop or get help: Do not let the Aid guess between two targets on consequential screens such as payments or health forms. Asking is the safety feature, not a flaw.

title: Signature Trusted-Caller Guard

title: Signature First-Day Setup Kit
body:
The Signature First-Day Setup Kit is an original Signature design for the whole first session with a new device, packaged as a guided checklist that a helper and user walk together: text, sound, favourites, messages, photos, and a printed guide, each tested with a real task before the next begins. The Kit refuses to rush: it suggests a break when the session passes half an hour, saves progress, and resumes another day without losing place. It ends by printing the large-print guide and scheduling a one-week check-in. The design is labeled Signature throughout.

How to do it: Guide text, sound, favourites, messages, photos, and guide in order; Test each step with a real task; Suggest a break after half an hour and save progress; Print the large-print guide at the end; Schedule a one-week check-in.

What to check: Test the Kit with a brand-new device and a first-time user, and confirm all three core tasks work unaided before the helper leaves.

When to stop or get help: Do not declare setup complete while any core task still needs help. A Kit that signs off early creates a drawer device.

Put it into practice on a small, low-stakes example first, so the routine is familiar before you need it under pressure. For this record, that means trying the steps once in a calm moment, with no deadline and no audience, and noticing which step feels hardest. The hardest step is usually the one worth practising twice, because pressure does not create new skills, it reveals the ones you have already rehearsed. Write down what you checked and what you found, because a check that leaves no note is hard to repeat and harder to trust later, and because a short note lets someone else pick up where you left off.

Share the routine with the people who will use it with you, so that stopping, checking, and asking for help are normal steps, not signs of failure. Agree in advance what you will do when a check fails, so that a failed check leads to a pause and a fix rather than an argument or a quiet decision to carry on anyway. Review the routine after a month of use and change the parts that did not work in practice, keeping the parts that did. A routine that is reviewed stays alive; a routine that is never reviewed slowly becomes a poster on a wall.
demo_code:
steps = ['text', 'sound', 'favourites', 'messages', 'photos', 'guide']
done = ['text', 'sound', 'favourites', 'messages', 'photos', 'guide']
print('kit steps:', len(steps))
print('steps completed:', len(done))
print('first day complete:', done == steps)
demo_output:
kit steps: 6
steps completed: 6
first day complete: True

title: Signature Family-Window Caller
body:
The Signature Family-Window Caller is an original Signature design for video calls reduced to a window: one screen, family faces, one tap to answer, and a gentle recovery that rejoins automatically if the call drops. It uses a regular call time so the window opens when family is expected, keeps the charger reminder visible, and falls back to an ordinary voice call after two failed video attempts, without asking the user to diagnose anything. The design is labeled Signature throughout.

How to do it: One screen with family faces and one-tap answer; Regular call time so calls are expected; Automatic rejoin after a drop; Voice-call fallback after two failed video attempts; Charger reminder visible during calls.

What to check: Test the Caller with a dropped call and two failed video attempts, and confirm it rejoins once and then falls back to voice without user diagnosis.

When to stop or get help: Do not keep retrying video indefinitely while a voice call would connect. Connection matters more than picture quality.

title: Signature Clinic-Door Guide
body:
The Signature Clinic-Door Guide is an original Signature design for health-app access as a single door: one tile for the clinic's app, saved login, a rehearsal mode for video visits, and a large phone-fallback button that is always visible. It writes the visit steps in large print, keeps the clinic's real number beside the tile, and never offers health advice itself: it opens the door to clinicians, and any worrying result routes to a phone call, not to a screen. The design is labeled Signature throughout, and it gives access skills, not medical advice.

How to do it: One tile for the clinic app with saved login; Rehearsal mode for video visits; Large phone-fallback button always visible; Large-print visit steps; Worrying results route to a phone call.

What to check: Test the Guide with a rehearsal visit and a simulated failed login, and confirm the fallback button reaches the clinic number in both cases.

When to stop or get help: Do not let the Guide interpret results or suggest treatments. Its door opens to clinicians, and it must never pretend to be one.

title: Signature App-Tryout Bench
body:
The Signature App-Tryout Bench is an original Signature design for trying assistive apps safely: it runs a candidate app in a trial week against one real task, scores it on large-text support, privacy, cost, and solo use, and shows the scorecard in large print before any purchase or account is offered. Apps that demand payment or broad permissions before proving value are set aside automatically, and the Bench keeps only winners, deleting the rest with their data. The design is labeled Signature throughout.

How to do it: Trial week against one real task; Scorecard on large text, privacy, cost, and solo use; Large-print scorecard before purchase or account; Set aside apps demanding early payment or broad permissions; Delete losers with their data.

What to check: Test the Bench with three candidate apps, one good and two demanding, and confirm only the good app survives the week with a passing scorecard.

When to stop or get help: Do not approve an app that fails privacy or demands payment before proving value, however good its description sounds. The scorecard decides, not the advertisement.

title: Signature Patient-Teacher Routine
body:
The Signature Patient-Teacher Routine is an original Signature design for teaching as a repeatable method: one skill, one reason, a slow demonstration, immediate practice, a jointly written large-print step card, and short repeat sessions across a week. The Routine watches for frustration and prescribes a break and a return to something enjoyable, because it treats confidence as the curriculum and the skill as its by-product. Teachers using the Routine record which steps worked, so the next teacher starts from success, not from scratch. The design is labeled Signature throughout.

How to do it: One skill and one reason per lesson; Slow demonstration then immediate practice; Jointly written large-print step card; Short repeats across a week; Frustration triggers a break, not pressure; Record what worked for the next teacher.

What to check: Test the Routine across three learners and one skill each, and confirm all three perform the skill unaided a week later.

When to stop or get help: Do not push through frustration to finish a lesson. A lesson that ends badly teaches avoidance, which is harder to undo than any skill is to learn.

Put it into practice on a small, low-stakes example first, so the routine is familiar before you need it under pressure.
